source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Minimum description length
finding: Algorithmic MDL: the description length of data is the length of the smallest program that outputs it. This is Kolmogorov complexity, tied to Solomonoff's theory of induction. It cannot be computed. Statistical MDL (Rissanen) uses a code that is not computationally universal, so in principle it cannot learn models of recursive natural processes.
numbers: Rissanen 1978 (Automatica 14(5):465-471) is the first statistical MDL; Wallace and Boulton MML 1968; 1000-coin-flip example: 510 heads and 490 tails gives too little evidence for bias once the full model cost is counted.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, read through a fetch tool summary; gives no LLM results.
agent_relevance: Defines the split we need: ideal algorithmic MDL (universal, incomputable) versus practical MDL (computable, weaker language). Our agent can only use a practical proxy.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Minimum description length: Minsky remark
finding: The article reports that on 14 Dec 2014 Marvin Minsky called algorithmic probability (Chaitin, Solomonoff, Kolmogorov) the most important discovery since Goedel, and said practical approximations could beat current predictors.
numbers: Date: 14 December 2014, World Science Festival panel.
limits: Opinion, not data. Reported second-hand.
agent_relevance: Motivation only; no test.

source: Grunwald (2004) A Tutorial Introduction to the Minimum Description Length Principle
finding: Ideal MDL: Kolmogorov complexity K(D) is the length of the shortest program that prints D and halts. Invariance theorem: two general-purpose languages differ by at most a constant c that does not depend on the length of D. Kolmogorov (1965), Chaitin (1969) and Solomonoff (1964) found it independently.
numbers: The constant c does not grow with data length, but for short data it can dominate.
quote: for every two general-purpose programming languages A and B ... differ by no more than a constant c
limits: Tutorial. The original papers (Solomonoff 1964, Kolmogorov 1965, Chaitin 1969) were not opened here.
agent_relevance: The base language (our prompt, tool set, DSL) is the 'constant'. With few examples (ARC has 2 to 5 pairs) that constant can decide the answer.

source: Grunwald (2004) Tutorial: why ideal MDL is not used
finding: Ideal MDL has two defects in practice. (1) Uncomputability: no program returns the shortest program for every D. (2) Arbitrariness: for small samples the chosen hypothesis depends on syntax details of the language.
numbers: Two named defects. Practical MDL fixes both by restricting the description language.
limits: Argument, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Both defects apply to an LLM agent: it cannot prove a program is shortest, and its pick depends on its wording. Treat 'shortest' as a ranking heuristic, never as proof (fits G3).

source: Grunwald (2004) Tutorial: crude versus refined MDL
finding: Crude (two-part) MDL picks the hypothesis H minimising L(H)+L(D|H). Refined MDL replaces this with one universal code per model class (NML, minimax optimal), with parametric complexity COMP(H) measuring how well the class fits random data.
numbers: L(H) in crude MDL is hard to define fairly; refined MDL removes that arbitrary choice.
limits: Statistical MDL; the code is not Turing-universal.
agent_relevance: For S7-style choice between candidate programs, a two-part score (program length plus misfit on examples) is the usable crude form.

source: Grunwald (2004) Tutorial: MDL as Occam's razor
finding: The tutorial treats MDL as a precise form of Occam's razor: trade goodness of fit against complexity. For large samples the crude criterion matches BIC.
numbers: Sections 1.4 to 1.6 and 2.10.
limits: Conceptual; the claim that simpler models generalize better depends on the model class.
agent_relevance: A short program that fits is evidence only if the program language is fixed in advance and not tuned to the examples (reinforces G3).

source: Rathmanner and Hutter (2011) A Philosophical Treatise of Universal Induction
finding: Solomonoff induction mixes all computable hypotheses with weight 2^-length. The sum of its prediction errors is bounded by a constant that depends on the prior weight of the true source (of order ln of 1/w). So errors are finite for any computable world.
numbers: Bound grows as the true source gets smaller prior weight; if the prior weight is 1 the bound is zero.
limits: Incomputable. The bound assumes the world is computable and the prior dominates the true source.
agent_relevance: This is the theory behind 'prefer short programs': one prior with a no-regret guarantee. Practical agents approximate it with a bias to short code.

source: Rathmanner and Hutter (2011): no free lunch versus Occam
finding: No-free-lunch theorems assume simple and complex worlds are equally likely. The authors call this absurd for the real world. Solomonoff induction assumes only that some structure exists, without naming which.
numbers: Section 2.5; Mitchell's inductive-learning assumption is called circular (Hume).
quote: If every raven we have ever seen has been black, does it really seem equally plausible
limits: Philosophical argument; the simplicity bias is assumed, not tested.
agent_relevance: Justifies a simplicity preference as a stated assumption in the schema (a design choice [D], not an established fact).

source: Hutter (2000) A Theory of Universal Artificial Intelligence based on Algorithmic Complexity (AIXI)
finding: Combines Solomonoff induction with sequential decision theory into a parameterless agent, argued to be the most intelligent unbiased agent. It is uncomputable. A time and space bounded version, AItl, is as good as any agent bounded by time t and space l.
numbers: AItl computation time is of order t * 2^l.
limits: Time of order t*2^l is not usable in practice; the claim is theoretical.
agent_relevance: Frames the ceiling: even the ideal agent is a short-program searcher. Practical approximations trade guarantees for speed.

source: Schmidhuber (2002) Optimal Ordered Problem Solver (OOPS)
finding: Levin search tests programs with a runtime limit proportional to program probability, doubling the budget each phase. It is only a constant factor slower than the best program. OOPS adds incremental reuse of earlier solutions.
numbers: Towers of Hanoi with 30 disks (solution above 10^9 moves) solved; reuse of a prefix sped up the search by a factor of 1000.
limits: The constant factor P(p) can be huge; only toy domains.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule for allocating attempts: spend budget in proportion to prior plausibility (short first), double the cap on failure. Matches a counted, code-controlled budget.

source: Chollet (2019) On the Measure of Intelligence
finding: Defines intelligence as skill-acquisition efficiency, using Algorithmic Information Theory. Priors and experience must be controlled, since unlimited data can 'buy' skill. Introduces ARC, whose tasks are meant to be solved from a few examples.
numbers: Definition and benchmark proposal; ARC tasks give few demonstration pairs.
limits: Definition, not an empirical law.
agent_relevance: Supports scoring our agent on few-example tasks with stated priors, and reading a short program as evidence of generalization.

source: Ellis et al. (2020) DreamCoder: wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Learns a library of reusable routines by compressing solved programs (an MDL/Bayes objective: library description length plus program description lengths). Wake: search programs. Sleep-abstraction: refactor to compress. Sleep-dreaming: train a neural guide.
numbers: List processing: 218 tasks, 50/50 split, 15 examples each; about 20 new routines learned. Text editing: 3.7% solved before learning, 79.6% after, in 40 s versus 235 s. CVC4 solved 82.4% with 1 hour and 8 CPUs; DreamCoder 84.3% with that budget (108 SyGuS problems).
limits: Training takes about a day on 20-100 CPUs; needs a hand-built starting language.
agent_relevance: Core idea for S2/S7: reward programs by length after reuse. A learned library shrank search time about 6x here.

source: Ellis et al. (2020) DreamCoder: ablations and physics
finding: All three parts help (library with refactoring, recognition model, and memorisation baselines are worse). In generative domains (LOGO graphics, tower building) no baseline solves over 60% of held-out tasks while DreamCoder solves nearly 100%.
numbers: Mean search time 54.1 s, median 15.0 s. From generic primitives (map, fold, arithmetic) it learns 93% of 60 physics laws after 8 wake/sleep cycles; vector algebra and an inverse-square law emerge.
limits: Authors' own benchmarks; clean task specifications.
agent_relevance: Compression-driven abstraction can discover vocabulary, not only answers. For us: reuse of earlier sub-solutions as named parts.

source: Lake, Salakhutdinov and Tenenbaum (2015) Human-level concept learning through probabilistic program induction (BPL)
finding: Bayesian program learning represents handwritten characters as probabilistic stroke programs. One-shot classification reached human level and beat deep nets; visual Turing tests found judges mostly could not tell machine from human output.
numbers: Search-result summary only (PDF fetch gave HTTP 403): Science 350(6266):1332-1338. Exact error rates not verified.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite numbers until read. Omniglot is a clean toy domain.
agent_relevance: Classic case of a program-like prior plus Bayes giving one-shot learning. Unverified here.

source: Deletang et al. (2024, ICLR) Language Modeling Is Compression
finding: A predictive model plus arithmetic coding is a lossless compressor, so log-loss equals code length. Large LMs are strong general compressors even outside text.
numbers: Chinchilla 70B compresses ImageNet patches to 43.4% and LibriSpeech to 16.4% of raw size, beating PNG 58.5% and FLAC 30.3%. On enwik9, Chinchilla 70B raw 8.3%, Llama 2 7B 8.9%, gzip 32.3%.
limits: Raw rates ignore model size. Counting parameters (a two-part code), Chinchilla 70B is 21.9% on enwik9 but 185.3% on ImageNet and 228.9% on LibriSpeech.
agent_relevance: Ties an LLM's loss to description length. Counting the model size is exactly the two-part cost; a big model only pays off on big data.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Scaling and tokenization as compression
finding: Adjusted compression of Transformers trained on enwik8 has an optimal model size per dataset size: bigger models help only on bigger data and get worse on small data. Tokenization is itself compression.
numbers: Table 2, raw rate on enwik9 for the 38M-parameter model: ASCII 6.4%, BPE 10K 7.4%, BPE 20K about 8.7 to 9.0% (simpler tokenizers compress better, but large vocabularies pack more into the context).
limits: Models trained on enwik8 only; offline two-part accounting.
agent_relevance: Scaling laws depend on test-set size once the model cost is counted. Bigger is not always a shorter total description.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Compressors as generative models and in-context compression
finding: Any compressor (even gzip) can be turned into a conditional generative model. The in-context view says an LM adapts to a task through its context, a form of online compression.
numbers: Out of domain: Transformers trained on enwik8 compress similar Wikipedia-style text well but fail on images and audio.
limits: Gzip-generated samples are poor.
agent_relevance: Supports treating in-context examples as data the model is compressing; no extra mechanism needed.

source: Grau-Moya, Genewein, Hutter et al. (2024) Learning Universal Predictors
finding: Trains neural nets on data from random programs run on a universal Turing machine (BrainPhoque), an approximation of the Solomonoff prior. Larger models give lower cumulative regret; Transformers trained on UTM data transfer best to Chomsky-hierarchy tasks, LSTMs to variable-order Markov sources.
numbers: UTM data: programs run 1000 steps, 200 memory cells, outputs of length 256. 500K iterations, batch 128, 3 seeds, sizes S/M/L, 6k eval sequences. All models beat a loose Solomonoff upper bound. Longer underlying program means higher regret.
limits: Transformers fail at length generalisation (trained 256, tested 1024); LSTMs do better. The upper bound is loose.
agent_relevance: Program length predicts prediction difficulty, as the theory says. Program-generated training data gives transferable patterns, but only within the trained length.

source: Grau-Moya et al. (2024) Variable-order Markov and Chomsky results
finding: On variable-order Markov sources, where the Bayes-optimal predictor is Context Tree Weighting, Transformer-L matches the optimal predictor and LSTM-L is close. This suggests the nets implement a Bayesian mixture over programs or trees.
numbers: 15 Chomsky tasks (400 sequences each, 6k total); Transformer-L best in distribution; models struggle on mid-sized context lengths.
limits: Toy sources; matching CTW does not show general Solomonoff behaviour.
agent_relevance: In-context learners can act as Bayesian mixtures over simple programs, which supports using several samples plus checks rather than one guess.

source: Huang, Zhang, Shan and He (2024, COLM) Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly
finding: Across 31 public LLMs and 12 benchmarks, average benchmark score is almost linear in bits per character on external corpora.
numbers: Pearson about -0.95 per domain; per benchmark -0.881 (HellaSwag), -0.951 (TriviaQA), -0.946 (DS-1000), -0.930 (MMLU case).
limits: Base models only; short to medium context; may not hold for models where the ability has not emerged yet.
agent_relevance: A cheap unsupervised proxy: lower code length on in-domain text goes with higher skill. Useful for choosing a model, not for scoring one answer.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Boundary: the corpus must match the ability
finding: When the compression corpus does not match the skill, the linear link is much weaker: math benchmarks against Common Crawl, and knowledge benchmarks against GitHub code.
numbers: Exact weaker Pearson values are in the paper's Figure 6 (not read as numbers).
limits: In-domain alignment is required; fine-tuned models excluded.
agent_relevance: Description length measures only what it is computed on. Our agent must compress the actual task data, not generic text.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: A 76K-parameter network trained only at inference time on the single target puzzle, by minimising description length (KL of a latent code plus reconstruction cross-entropy), with no pretraining and no ARC training set.
numbers: 20% of ARC-AGI-1 evaluation puzzles (2 guesses) and 34.75% of training puzzles; 2000 steps, about 20 minutes per puzzle. Training set, first-guess accuracy: 100 steps 1.0%, 500 steps 23.0%, 1000 steps 28.0%, 2000 steps 30.25%.
quote: Despite never using the training set, performing no pretraining
limits: Cannot do counting, color assignment, rotation or reflection, connectivity, planning, or long-range pattern extension. Slow (about 130 h for the training set on one RTX 4070).
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that raw MDL at test time solves a real share of ARC. Strong where symmetry and repetition help, weak where rules need counting or search.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) CompressARC: context against other ARC methods
finding: The paper lists other approaches for context: brute-force rule search 40% (private eval), HRM-style model trained on train plus test puzzles 40.3%, and a large pretrained LLM system 87.5% (semi-private eval). It also lists a 31% figure for CompressARC when counting the test puzzles.
numbers: Rows quoted from the text: 40%, 40.3%, 87.5%, 31%. A U-Net baseline trained on the target puzzle is listed but its row is garbled in the extracted text.
limits: Table layout lost in extraction; verify before citing the U-Net row.
agent_relevance: Puts MDL-only learning (20%) in context: far below LLM-with-search but with no pretraining.

source: Yoran et al. (2025, ICLR) The KoLMogorov Test: Compression by Code Generation
finding: Benchmark asks a code model to write the shortest program that outputs a given sequence (audio, text, DNA, synthetic). Prompted flagship models mostly fail.
numbers: Llama-3.1-405B fails 78% and GPT-4o 40% of the time on natural data; 66% and 45% on synthetic data. All prompted models have precision above 1.0 (programs longer than the gzip output).
limits: Gzip is not tuned for Python programs. Correct programs on natural data are more than 95% simple repetitions.
agent_relevance: Measured gap: LLMs are poor program compressors. Do not trust a model's claim of a 'shortest' program; check by running it.

source: Yoran et al. (2025) KT: trained SeqCoder and generalisation
finding: 1.5B-parameter code models trained on synthetic program-sequence pairs beat prompted models by over 40% on synthetic data but do poorly on real data. A uniform prior over the DSL beats gzip.
numbers: Over 99% of programs from the 10K-example model err in the first 16 characters; 93.5% and 88.7% for 100K and 1M examples. In over 30% of failures models split the input into sub-sequences and merge them with subtle errors.
limits: Gains on synthetic data generalize poorly to real data; counting errors are common. Execution feedback gave only modest gains.
agent_relevance: Program writing needs run-and-check; inline feedback helps only a little, so the check must come from code, not the model.

source: Wang, Gao, Pu, Haber and Goodman (2024, ICLR) Hypothesis Search
finding: GPT-4 proposes abstract natural-language hypotheses, then implements each as Python and verifies it on the examples. Both abstract hypotheses and concrete programs help.
numbers: 100-problem ARC subset: direct prompting 17%; hypotheses plus programs 23%; with LLM summary of hypotheses 30%; with human selection from candidates 33%. Without programs GPT-4 dropped to 19%. Of 49 tasks with selected hypotheses, 33 (67%) led to correct programs. SyGuS: 94.3% with 8 programs.
limits: Top-1 scoring here, not top-3. Small subset. Human selection needed for the 33%.
agent_relevance: Program-form hypotheses that can be executed against examples beat direct answers. Matches our verify-before-trust rule.

source: Grau-Moya et al. (2024) and Deletang et al. (2024): shared length limit
finding: Both lines of work show learned compressors work inside the context length and training length. Beyond it, performance falls.
numbers: Transformers trained at length 256 fail at 1024 (Grau-Moya et al.); gzip context 32 KB versus Transformer context 2048 bytes (Deletang et al.).
limits: Different tasks; the link is our synthesis, not a direct test.
agent_relevance: Long tasks need chunking and written-out intermediate programs rather than one long in-context compression.
